messages.content: Each section must begin with a thesis statement in italics, use HTML to indicate the italics. Write a story about a hedgehog with glasses, the only real creature in an abstract world, resembling abstract art

message.content: In a world of color and form, the small prickly creature with round spectacles was the only thing that bled, the only thing that breathed, the only thing that cast a shadow not made of pigment. He stepped carefully across a field of cadmium yellow, the paint beneath his quills thick and ridged, still wet in places where no one had ever walked. The horizon was not a line but a suggestion—a bleeding of ultramarine into raw umber where some absent painter had let the colors argue with each other. There were no trees. There were no birds. There was only the surface, the layer upon layer of gesture, the smudge where a brush had been dragged in impatience. The hedgehog adjusted his glasses—thin wire frames, slightly too large for his snout, held on by a tiny screw at the hinge—and pressed forward. Each footfall left a print in the still-drying gesso, and the print was *real* in a way the gesso was not. The gesso would never itch. The gesso would never feel the damp. Everywhere the hedgehog turned his gaze, the world was composition: blocks of color, arcs of gesture, the absence of narrative. To his left, a great vertical band of vermillion stood against a field of black—not a building, not a cliff, but a *feeling* made solid, the way a Rothko knew how to make a feeling stand where a wall should be. To his right, the ground erupted in a storm of white and gray and thin black lines, a web of splatter that had no center and no edge, a Pollock canvas poured out across the earth. Further on, a grid of primary colors divided the plain into rectangles the way Mondrian had divided silence into its smallest honest pieces. The hedgehog walked along the borders between these regions, because the borders were where the paint was thinnest, where his little paws were least likely to sink into some still-liquid pool of alizarin crimson. He did not look up. There was no sky. Only a great smear of pale blue-gray, flat as a ceiling, with a single drip of titanium white running down it like a vein. The glasses were the first thing he remembered making, and the first thing he would keep. He had not made them. He had found them in a small hollow where the paint pooled low and glistened, a tiny workshop of nothing where a brush-stroke had accidentally formed a loop, a rim, a lens. He had picked them up and put them on, and the world had *narrowed*, and in that narrowing, he had become a *who*. Without the glasses, he was just a small dark shape with quills, easily mistaken for a smudge of charcoal, a stray mark the painter hadn't meant to make. With the glasses, he was a character. He was the protagonist of a story no one else was reading. The lenses were slightly convex, and they made the abstract world *look* like a world—gave the color-fields a depth they didn't have, gave the splatters a perspective that made them seem like they were *happening* somewhere. A small magic. A small lie. And he was grateful for both. He walked because stopping meant becoming a still life, and a still life in an abstract world was just another shape. Days did not pass. There was no sun to track, no arc of light to measure the hours. But he walked because his paws ached in the stillness, and because the quills at the base of his neck—softer than the others, almost like the down of a bird—twitched with a restlessness that had no name in a world with no words. The world had no words. There were no signs. There were no labels. There was only the *gesture*, the *mark*, the *relationship between one color and another*. The hedgehog walked through a region where the paint was thrown in thin, violent arcs, a de Kooning of raw violence, and his heart hammered and his breathing quickened, and for a moment he forgot he was the only real thing. He simply *was*, and the world was, and the distinction between them was a thin and useless line. A quill caught on a ridge of dried impasto and he hissed, and the hissing was a sound no one had ever made in this place, and the sound *changed* the paint where it struck the surface, making a tiny dimple, a tiny *real* dent in the abstract, and he walked faster. He understood, at last, that the abstract world was not empty. It was waiting. It waited in the way a half-finished canvas waits—not with hope, but with *potential*. The color-fields did not need him. The splatters did not need a witness. The grid of primaries was complete and would be complete whether he walked it or not. And yet. And yet. There was a place, a great way at the center of the ultramarine-umber suggestion, where the paint was very thin and very old and very still, and where, if he looked with his round wire spectacles, he could see a small, pale shape that was almost a figure, almost a *self*, almost a creature with a snout and quills and the faintest suggestion of a pair of tiny glasses. It was there the way a signature is there—barely, in the corner, in the lightest hand. The hedgehog walked toward it. The paint beneath his paws was dry and hard and *old*, and it did not smear, and it did not change, and it did not make a sound when he stepped on it. And he thought: *I am the only thing here that was not painted. I am the only thing here that is not a mark made by a hand. I am the only thing here that can look back.* And he looked. And the small pale shape in the thin old paint looked back. And neither of them was a painting. And both of them were. And the hedgehog put a small paw on the small pale shape's small pale paw, and the paint held, and the paw held, and the glasses fogs, and the world was still just color and form and gesture, but now, in the center of it, there was a small, warm, *real* pressure of one thing against another, and that was not a color. That was not a line. That was not a brushstroke. That was a *contact*, and it was the only real thing that had ever happened in the abstract world, and it was enough. It was, in fact, the whole point. The whole, small, prickly, glass-eyes point. And the hedgehog walked on, because walking was the only thing that was not a composition, and because his paws ached, and because the quills at the base of his neck twitched, and because the world was still painting itself, slowly, in the blue-gray smear overhead, and he wanted to see what it would become when it was done. And he walked. And the paint, beneath him, was patient. And the world, which was not a world, which was a *surface*, held him. And he was the only one who was not a mark. And he was enough. And he was, in the end, the only real creature in an abstract world, and the abstract world, in the end, was enough. And the glasses fogged. And he walked on.
